why_sota_failed: CORE TECHNICAL: the value-of-computation (VOC) selector reduces to a deadline test. Proposition 1 (paper/aamas2027/main.tex §4.4) shows that for theta>0 and pi<1, V_j(D)>0 exactly when b_yes(D)>0. With verdict bids (p_bar>=0.95) that is just D<slack. Two design choices cause this. First, there is no per-query cost term: judge_query_cost defaults to 0 (cbja/config.py), so delay is the only cost. Second, rival persistence pi=(4+K)/(5+K+L) is always below 1, so the rival-pruning branch never fires. Measured consequences: on 60 prespecified unused seeds (5300-5359), CBJA minus the incremental deadline rule was +0.11 (90% CI [-0.06,0.27]) in combined and +0.17 ([-0.08,0.42]) in contested, equivalent within +/-0.5 by TOST. Over ~1.2M decisions CBJA picked a different query set from the bulk filter only 1.1% (combined) and 1.4% (contested) of the time (appendix/generated/v8_power.tex).

The components that made CBJA novel did nothing measurable. Removing refresh, the batch externality, rival persistence, the value magnitude or the rival term changed the score by |delta|<=0.2 points (appendix v9_mechanism). In the synthetic-judge ablation they were identical to the last digit, because alpha and beta were small relative to slack. On the shared server the batch externality was also null (CBJA minus no_batch_cost: -0.1 / +1.7, n.s.). The only component that mattered was the delay term (no_delay costs 3.3* / 2.4* points, and 6.8* / 9.5* on the shared server). Any deadline-aware rule has that term.

The 'judgment-aware' bidding was dropped. Expected-value bids b=p*u-(1-p)*c lost whenever the judge was accurate: with real Kev on 12 seeds, probability bids scored -11.2 against independent while Boolean bids scored +4.7; with a perfect synthetic judge the loss was -14.7 [-25.7,-5.2]. The final CBJA uses verdict bids 1[p>=0.5]. It is therefore essentially CBBA plus a no-text shortcut plus a deadline-aware incremental batch.

The project's own judge result removed the regime where CBJA helps. CBJA leads the other auctions by 1.9-3.7 points only at 1-8 s per text, and ties again at 16 s. The fine-tuned judges run at 0.13-0.24 s per text on 4 CPU cores. At <=0.5 s no auction differs significantly from CBJA (|delta|<=1 in combined).

Early 'wins' came from uneven engineering and disappeared once baselines got the same infrastructure. The no-text shortcut was CBJA-only until v5: giving it to CBBA raised CBBA from 9.2% to 22.6% at 8 s/text, and the v3 claim of +21 to +95 raw points over the best other allocator collapsed to ties or +0.4-9.4. Other artifacts: a cost-unit bug (task vs text, worth +20-31 on the shared server), a Boolean-bid outlook bug (~260k 'wait' decisions per 10 missions), and delay estimates that counted queueing twice. Each engine fix invalidated earlier numbers (docs/cbja-results.md §8, §11-13).

CBJA did not lead once scale or scenario changed. At 16 robots it trailed CBBA when jammed (-48.3 raw, significant) and Independent under severe links (-64.0, significant). In the GPU contested zone SSI beat it by -35.3 [-63.2,-9.2]. On the shared server the central planner scored 58.5% against CBJA's 45.4% (p=.055); before the cost-unit fix CBJA was the weakest distributed allocator with packed calls (-32 to -70). At 32 robots with ideal links it trailed Independent by -44.3 (0/3 seeds). The fair station baseline (hybrid with local fallback) trails CBJA significantly only under severe links with GPU judges (+8.0*).

EVALUATION DESIGN: there was no established benchmark and no public numbers to beat. The problem (text notices gating task permission) was defined by the authors, and the self-built 2D discrete-event testbed was the only place it was evaluated. The repo's own survey (docs/benchmark-baseline-survey-2026-09.md) concluded that no public benchmark covers dynamic deadlines, changing semantic constraints, partial communication and portability together. A SOTA claim on a self-defined task can only be checked against the authors' own baselines.

The baselines were in-house partial adaptations, and some were weak. 'CBBA' gossips each robot's whole bid row with freshness fusion (cbja/simulation.py _receive, cbja/published.py fuse_record) and takes argmax over rows with a bundle limit of 3; it does not use CBBA's per-task winner/bid/timestamp tables or update/reset rules. SSI is the same engine with bundle limit 1. CC-OPI* and AC-DMTA* are labelled partial adaptations. The central planner (cbja/central.py) is a weak baseline: greedy one-task-per-robot assignment, robots idle without station contact, and it learns tasks only from robot status reports. The official CC-OPI code, cited as https://github.com/bdathe-lb/CC-OPI-Exp in arXiv 2609.19208, returned HTTP 404 when checked on 2026-09-27. The CV-MRTA code (https://github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark) has no reuse license. So no baseline could be run from official code.

The missions left little room for any allocator to win, and there was no optimum to compare against. Each mission has 8 robots, 24 tasks and 90-120 s. With ideal links every method earns 68-71% of total reward and about 7.6 of 24 tasks expire whatever the allocator (runs/highfreq-v5/rows.jsonl). An error-free, zero-time judge oracle adds only +0.4 to +0.9 points (appendix v8_oracle). The repo contains no MILP, Hungarian or other offline optimum (grep finds no solver). Allocator effects were therefore bounded at a few points, and the decentralized auctions stayed within about 2 points of each other everywhere.

Statistical power and scale were too low for a SOTA claim. Cells have 10-20 seeds; the 16- and 32-robot results have 5 and 3 seeds. The pure-Python engine re-decides on every message and broadcasts full row and task tables to every peer. An 8-robot mission produces about 16k messages and 43 MB and takes 8-25 s of wall time. A 16-robot fleet_hot run produces about 280k messages and 570 MB, takes 200-330 s and needs about 4 GB of RAM. A 32-robot jammed run takes 35-130 min. Large teams, where MRTA SOTA papers are usually evaluated, were out of reach.

The language component was synthetic and narrow. It uses 19 label specifications and 4 capabilities; all texts were written by models and labels were checked by models. Kev fine-tuning loss reached 0.000 (runs/kev-ft/kev06s-ft.log). On 300 real NOTAM and NYC subway notices every judge fell to .50-.72 pooled; Qwen3-8B answered 'no' to 294 of 300. The claims about judges therefore do not transfer to real notices.

PROCESS: an LLM mock-review-to-experiment loop drove the work. About 11 benchmark versions (v1-v11) and ~18.8k v5 result rows were produced in roughly 5 days (git history 2026-09-23 to 09-27). Mock scores stayed around 5/10 from v1 to v7 because the root cause, CBJA being roughly equal to a simple rule, was structural; rigor rose each round while significance did not. A hand-designed scenario win (joint recovery: 20/20 vs 1/20 urgent completions, +28.5 [25.5,30.0]) sat alongside a null result on the broader SPACE-derived workload.

FRAMING: the large effects came from system architecture, not the allocation algorithm. Deciding locally under severe links gave CBJA minus central +26.8* (central keeps 40% of its ideal-link score, auctions 70-82%). Fine-tuning the judge gave +12.9 to +25.1 at equal latency, and the no-text shortcut +5.5 to +5.8. None of these belongs to CBJA, so the SOTA story became an analysis paper.

empirical_lessons: Large effects came from where decisions run. Under severe links (jamming, short range and 20% loss), the central planner whose robots idle without the station keeps 40% of its ideal-link score (27.6% of total reward), local auctions keep 70-82%, and the hybrid keeps 68%. CBJA minus central: +12.5* jammed, +20.4* short range, +26.8* severe. At 16 robots severe links: CBJA 42.7% vs central 22.4%. At 32 robots jammed (3 seeds): CBJA keeps 82% of its ideal-link score, central 51%.

Judge quality is the next-largest effect. At equal 0.49 s latency, fine-tuning Kev-0.6B raises net score by 12.9-25.1 points in 4 of 5 CPU families. A generative LLM on a robot CPU is unusable: the best auction with Qwen3-8B at 13.6 s scores 22.1-61.1 points below the reference, and most tasks expire. On a shared server the fine-tuned 4B judge with 4-text calls beats Qwen3-8B by 14-27 points for every allocator, mainly through throughput (33.1 vs 10.8 texts/s).

Cheap structural tricks beat clever selection. The no-text shortcut (skip the judge when no received text concerns a task) is worth 5.5-5.8 points to CBBA at 1-8 s per text, more than any query-selection difference. Being aware of judge delay at all is worth 2.4-3.3 points (dedicated judge) and 6.8-9.5 points (shared server). How the delay is used matters little: the incremental rule matched CBJA within +/-0.5.

Rejudging held tasks is the one structural choice that matters in the contested zone: forcing it is worth +0.87 [0.22,1.53] there (exploratory). The incremental deadline rule beats the bulk filter by +1.74 [0.98,2.50] in contested but only +0.52 [-0.13,1.16] (n.s.) in combined.

Negligible, all within +/-0.2 to 1 point and not significant: VOC magnitude, the rival term, rival persistence, batch externality, rival refresh, expected-value vs verdict bids (+2.5 / +1.3, n.s.), judging notices at the station vs on board (-1.6 to +1.9), fitting delay to service times (<=1.2), and a gate on stale answers (no change).

Allocator choice among decentralized auctions matters little. With ideal links every method earns 68-71%. CBJA is within 2 points of the best other auction everywhere. An error-free, zero-time judge oracle adds only +0.4 to +0.9 points to each allocator under ideal links. The missions do not let allocators separate.

Information propagation, not selection, limits robustness. In severe-link CBJA runs, 42 of 48 violations with GPU judges and 43 of 75 with CPU judges followed notices the robot never received. Notices are not relayed between robots, while bids gossip over multiple hops.

Central planning wins when links are good. With CPU-only robots and ideal links, the central planner leads CBJA by 4.5* points and the hybrid by 4.0*. On the shared GPU server the central planner (58.5%) beats CBJA (45.4%, p=.055) because it judges each text once instead of once per robot.

Violation cost is not priced by any allocator. Rescoring the severe-link runs with lambda=8 makes every mean negative (CBJA -10.9, CC-OPI -10.8, central -31.0). In the synthetic-judge study, expected-value bids with lambda=8 cut violations from 4.1 to 0.5 per mission, but the reward cost was 154 raw points.

Robots without a GPU are viable only with single-pass classifiers. On 4 Xeon cores: Kev-0.6B-ft terse 0.236 s, DeBERTa-B-ft 0.13 s, Kev-4B 5.14 s, Qwen3-8B 13.6 s, VLM 8.72 s. llama.cpp Q4 brings Qwen3-8B only to 10.0 s at lower accuracy. Naive int8 halves Kev latency but costs about 3 accuracy points.

Results on synthetic language do not transfer to real notices. On 300 real notices, pooled accuracy was Kev-0.6B-ft .717, terse .640, Kev-4B-ft .673, DeBERTa-B-ft .600, zero-shot NLI about .52, and Qwen3-8B .500 (it said 'no' to 294/300). Most errors were missed prohibitions.

Fixing the cost unit (charging per new text instead of per question) was the one real algorithmic gain: +20.8 on development seeds and +30.7 [12.4,46.9] raw on evaluation seeds on the shared server with packed calls. It helped because cached texts are free and one status report gates many tasks.
traps_to_avoid: Do not claim SOTA on a self-defined problem, a self-built simulator and self-implemented baselines. Reviewers will not accept it. Choose an established benchmark with official baseline code and published numbers first, and design the method around that benchmark's metric.

Do not give the proposed method infrastructure the baselines lack: shortcuts, caches, cost units, packing. In CBJA this inflated early gains from +21 to +95 raw points down to about 0-3 points once the no-text shortcut was shared. Build common infrastructure first, give it to every method, then compare.

Before building a sophisticated selector, check analytically whether it collapses to a simple rule. CBJA's VOC had no per-query cost and a persistence estimate that is always below 1, so it was provably a deadline test (Proposition 1). Log how often the fancy and simple methods make different decisions early: here only 1.1-1.4% of decisions differed.

Do not evaluate on missions without headroom or an upper bound. Every method scored 68-71% with ideal links, and a perfect judge added <1 point. Add an offline optimal or MILP bound (or at least a clairvoyant centralized bound), and tune the task load so that allocators can differ by more than noise.

Do not accept a hand-designed scenario win as evidence. The joint-recovery result (20/20 vs 1/20 urgent completions) disappeared on the broader SPACE-derived workload. Wins must hold on distributions you did not design.

Do not use a weak central baseline. Here robots idled without station contact, the planner dispatched one task per plan, and notices were not relayed while bids gossiped over multiple hops. A reviewer flags these first. Include a queue-dispatching central planner, a hybrid, and relay-enabled variants.

Do not let a mock-review loop drive experiments. v1-v7 mock scores stayed around 5/10 because the problem was structural; each round added rigor and text but no significance. Decide the claim and benchmark up front and prespecify a confirmation block (the v10 TOST workflow is good practice).

Do not scale the old Python engine. It re-decides on every message and broadcasts full tables: about 16k messages and 43 MB per 8-robot mission, about 280k messages, 570 MB and 200-330 s per 16-robot run, and 35-130 min per 32-robot run. SOTA MRTA evaluation usually needs many more agents and instances; plan a vectorized or compiled engine, or adopt the benchmark's simulator.

Do not run underpowered cells. 5 seeds (16 robots) and 3 seeds (32 robots) produced no significant differences. Budget hundreds of paired instances (CV-MRTA uses 500 paired instances across 25 conditions) and power the headline contrast in advance.

Do not rely on model-written, model-checked evaluation language or on training loss near 0. Real notices collapsed every judge to .50-.72. If language stays in the new project, test on human-issued text from the start.

Do not change the engine mid-campaign without rerunning everything. Several engine fixes (abort on revoke, commit window, duplicate-claim yielding, text cost unit, Boolean-outlook bug) invalidated earlier tables, and old numbers kept leaking into drafts.

Licensing and code availability: CV-MRTA (https://github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark) has no reuse license, so only its protocol can be reused without contacting the authors. The CC-OPI official repo cited in arXiv 2609.19208 (https://github.com/bdathe-lb/CC-OPI-Exp) returned 404 on 2026-09-27 (unverified whether it will be released). SPACE is GPL-3.0, so copying its code forces GPL.

Compute: the older memory note (about 19.2 CPUs, 82 GB) is outdated. On 2026-09-27 the cgroup reports cpu.max 9600000/100000 = 96 CPUs and memory.max of about 1.2 TiB, with 4 idle H100s. Always set torch thread counts, because nproc reports 224 host CPUs. Launch long jobs with setsid nohup. Never pkill -f with a pattern that matches your own shell.
Evaluation-text provenance: LLMs wrote the evaluation texts. Never describe them as author-written (memory note from the AAMAS submission).
promising_unexplored_directions_from_rep: The paper's stated next step (main.tex, Discussion): allocators that price verdict error and information age, deciding whether to hold a task, ask again, or defer to the station. The CBJA VOC deliberately ignored judge error (theta is the probability of a permitting verdict, not of permission), and 42/48 severe-link violations came from missing notices. A selector with an error-aware, information-age-aware value, including a real query cost so that it does not collapse to a deadline test, is still untested.

Signed notice relaying through peers. Notices currently reach robots only over station links, while bids already gossip over multiple hops. The network already has relay machinery through the station (Network._send_relay / _relay_hop in /home/jovyan/dev/cbja/cbja/network.py) but not peer-to-peer notice forwarding. Prior art to cite and beat: CBBA with Relays (Ponda, Johnson, Kopeikin, Choi, How, IEEE JSAC 2012; https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6214698, verified via search). Since most severe-link violations follow notices that were never received, this is the most direct lever the repo identifies.

Risk-aware or chance-constrained bidding. Rescoring with lambda=8 made every allocator negative, so none prices violation cost well. Expected-value bids with a tuned lambda cut violations 4.1 to 0.5 per mission in the synthetic study, at a reward cost. Chance-constrained CBBA (Ponda 2012) and uncertainty-aware auctions (Rossano, Lim & How, arXiv 2509.22469, cited in refs.bib) are the relevant baselines.

Stronger station-side designs suggested by the mock review and the Limitations: a central planner that dispatches task queues instead of one task per plan; a server-side (text, version) answer cache shared by the auctions on the shared server, which could close the 58.5 vs 45.4 gap; and station interpretation broadcast to CPU robots, which already gave +10.4* under severe links.

Port to external benchmarks, as the repo's survey recommended (docs/benchmark-allocation-survey.md): first match baselines on the CV-MRTA protocol (Lott & Honary, arXiv 2609.13711, verified: CBAA, ACBBA, PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA; 500 paired ten-target instances x 25 communication conditions; Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott and Rayleigh loss); then use SPACE dynamic arrivals (GPL-3.0) and MRTA-250K / SADCHER heterogeneous and coalition instances (CC BY 4.0, 250k MILP-optimal schedules: https://data.4tu.nl/datasets/10e28ee0-9ad9-450d-8be7-6e6a91f2931f); optionally the League of Robot Runners 2026 scheduling track (https://pathfinding.ai/projects/league-of-robot-runners/). These have published numbers that the CBJA work never used.

Compare against CC-OPI on its own terms. CC-OPI (Liu & Zhang, arXiv 2609.19208, verified; submitted 2026-09-16) reports about 80% task completion at 250 m communication radius and about 7 points over matched online PI/CBBA baselines. Once its code is public, a method that beats it on its own simulator and seeds (reported seeds 42-71) would be a recognizable SOTA claim.

An upper-bound-anchored evaluation: add an offline MILP or clairvoyant centralized optimum to the existing generator, so that gap-to-optimal can be reported. The repo never measured how far 68-71% is from optimal.

Engine scale-up. The n^2 message flood and per-message re-decision capped experiments at 16-32 robots. A delta or material-change broadcast mode exists (broadcast_mode: material) but 'barely helped' under churn. Event batching, vectorization, or a GPU/JAX re-implementation of the link model would enable 50-200 robot evaluations at the scale where MRTA SOTA claims are made.

Learned or amortized selection versus rules. The only non-trivial selection structures that helped were incremental greedy batching and forced rejudging of held tasks. A learned policy (for example GNN or transformer allocators such as SADCHER, https://github.com/jakbichler/Sadcher) trained on the generator's distributions, with communication degradation as domain randomization, was never tried.

Verified external anchors (2026-09-27). CC-OPI (arXiv 2609.19208, Liu & Zhang, 2026-09-16): about 80% completion at 250 m radius, about 7 points over online PI/CBBA; code repo 404. CV-MRTA (arXiv 2609.13711, Lott & Honary, 2026-09-12): DGA and DMCHBA best MinMax (24.49 and 24.78 steps), HIPC best MinSum (66.95), compute from 4.88 ms (DMCHBA) to 1.346 s (DGA). AC-DMTA: Drones 10(7):523, 2026-07-09, https://doi.org/10.3390/drones10070523.

sweeps.area: Market/consensus-based DECENTRALIZED multi-robot task allocation (CBBA family, PI family, Hungarian-/GA-/game-theoretic decentralized allocators, and learned decentralized allocators), 2019-2026, with a focus on degraded communication and the optimality gap to centralized MILP. Sweep date 2026-09-27. How I verified: arXiv abs/html pages, Crossref metadata, the GitHub API, IOS Press/PMC pages, and full-text PDF extraction for the two key papers (Lott & Honary 2026, Dai et al. RA-L 2025). Anything marked UNVERIFIED I could not confirm from a primary source. Bottom line: nobody holds a single accepted SOTA here. Only three papers compare several method families on shared instances: Nayak et al. RA-L 2020, Cao et al. RA-L 2025 and Lott & Honary arXiv Sep-2026. They disagree, because the winner depends on the objective (MinMax vs MinSum), on communication quality and on the reliability/compute budget. Only one recent paper measures CBBA against a MILP optimum at scale (GACA 2026, CBBA at a median 81-84% of optimal), and it assumes full connectivity. Two naming corrections to the task text. In this literature 'DGA' in benchmarks means Decentralized GENETIC Algorithm (Patel et al., ICRA 2020). Distributed greedy is a different paper (Qu, Brown, Li, Automatica 2019). I could not identify any MRTA algorithm called 'LAPS' (UNVERIFIED / possibly nonexistent). Tooling note: the WebSearch budget ran out mid-sweep. The rest was verified with WebFetch, curl, Crossref and the GitHub API. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, and IEEE Xplore pages did not render.

sota_methods.name: CBBA (Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm)
sota_methods.key_idea: Each agent builds a bundle greedily by marginal gain (the auction phase). Agents then resolve conflicts by consensus on winning bids and timestamps. The result is conflict-free and converges in bounded rounds. Under diminishing marginal gains (DMG) the solution is guaranteed at least 50% of optimal.
sota_methods.problem: ST-SR-TA multi-task assignment (e.g., mTSP-like visit, time-discounted rewards)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Self-generated random instances in the original paper. It is the de facto baseline in almost every later paper.
sota_methods.reported_results: GACA 2026 (arXiv 2608.15884): CBBA reaches a median 81-84% of the MILP optimum on min-sum mTSP, 5-20 agents, 4,000 worlds. Cao et al. RA-L 2025 (per the IEEE abstract): CBBA was best in pre-allocation on reliability, overhead and efficiency, and gave the best optimality in dynamic allocation.
sota_methods.code_url: https://github.com/zehuilu/CBBA-Python (community implementation, 130 stars); CBBA is also inside https://github.com/Khaalex1/Global_Consensus_Based_Bundle_Algorithm
sota_methods.license: MIT (zehuilu/CBBA-Python); the GCBBA repo has no license file
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Myopic greedy insertion with no reallocation. Its scoring is poorly aligned with min-sum and min-max objectives. Kha et al. (ECAI 2025) show the time-discounted-reward score is not always DMG and that the 50% guarantee can fail even under DMG. It needs repeated consensus rounds, and conflicts and duplicates appear under packet loss (Rantanen et al., SECON 2019, DOI 10.1109/SAHCN.2019.8824898).

sota_methods.name: ACBBA (Asynchronous CBBA)
sota_methods.key_idea: An asynchronous version of CBBA with local deconfliction rules, so agents need no synchronized rounds.
sota_methods.problem: Asynchronous decentralized multi-task assignment
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Used as a baseline in Nayak RA-L 2020 and Lott & Honary 2026 (Collaborative Visit, CV)
sota_methods.reported_results: Lott & Honary 2026, mean MinMax over 24 impaired communication conditions: 26.91 steps (DGA 24.49, the best). In ideal pre-allocation it was stable in 98/100 runs. At Bernoulli p_drop=0.5 only 35/100 runs were viable and 9/100 stable.
sota_methods.license: The CV_MRTA_Benchmark repo has no license file (all rights reserved by default)
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Loses stability and viability quickly as packet loss grows. Rantanen et al. 2018/2019 report duplicate assignments and unassigned tasks in lossy networks.

sota_methods.name: PI (Performance Impact) and its descendants (PI-MaxAss / rescheduling / PI-infer-conv / efficient PI)
sota_methods.venue: IEEE T-Cybernetics 46(4):902-915 (PI); IROS 2015; IEEE T-Cyb 48(9) 2018; JAAMAS 37 2023; IEEE TIE 71(11) 2024; IEEE T-ASE 21 2024
sota_methods.key_idea: Bids use a task's 'performance impact' on the whole route: removal impact and inclusion impact rather than simple marginal gain. Agents alternate task removal and inclusion with consensus, which allows reallocation. Variants: Whitbrook et al. IROS 2015 (DOI 10.1109/IROS.2015.7354299) for time-critical scheduling. Turner et al. T-Cyb 2018 (DOI 10.1109/TCYB.2017.2743164) for distributed rescheduling to maximize the number of allocated tasks. Li et al. JAAMAS 2023 (DOI 10.1007/s10458-023-09611-y) add task-removal inference and deadlock avoidance, because PI can cycle forever exchanging the same task. Bai et al. TIE 2024 (DOI 10.1109/TIE.2024.3374366) add decoupled/coupled PI with global task inclusion and 1-opt. Wang et al. T-ASE 2024 (DOI 10.1109/TASE.2023.3281577).
sota_methods.problem: Multi-task assignment with deadlines (search-and-rescue), minimizing average task start time
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Self-built search-and-rescue scenarios. Also used as a baseline in Nayak 2020, Cao 2025, Lott 2026 and CC-OPI 2026.
sota_methods.reported_results: Original PI: beats CBBA on average rescue time and number of survivors assigned (qualitative abstract claim; numbers not extracted). Lott & Honary 2026: PI was the worst on MinMax under impaired communication (29.05 steps). Ideal pre-allocation: 97/100 viable, 70/100 stable. At Bernoulli 0.5: 18/100 viable, 3/100 stable.
sota_methods.code_url: No official code found on GitHub. Reimplementations: https://github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark; https://github.com/bdathe-lb/c4-mata-sim
sota_methods.license: c4-mata-sim is MIT; CV_MRTA_Benchmark has none
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Can fail to converge through a task-exchange cycle (the reason for the 2023 fix). Very fragile under packet loss. Most PI-variant papers compare only against PI/CBBA, on their own simulators, with no MILP reference.

sota_methods.name: HIPC (Hybrid Information and Plan Consensus)
sota_methods.venue: AIAA GNC 2013; Distributed Autonomous Robotic Systems, STAR vol. 112, 2016
sota_methods.key_idea: Each robot plans implicitly for a local team: it predicts the plans of neighbours whose state it knows and runs greedy team-level allocation over them. Plan consensus then removes the remaining conflicts. This cuts convergence time and message count.
sota_methods.problem: Decentralized multi-task assignment with reduced communication
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Nayak RA-L 2020; Lott & Honary 2026 CV benchmark
sota_methods.reported_results: Lott & Honary 2026: best mean MinSum under impaired communication, 66.95 steps (DGA 67.22). HIPC and DGA were the top two in every impaired condition. At Bernoulli p=0.5 pre-allocation it was still 100/100 viable and stable. Ideal median full-protocol computation C_term was 52.65 ms.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Relies on accurate peer-state prediction; the 2016 extension handles imperfect situational awareness. Weaker on MinMax: 25.12 steps vs 24.49 for DGA.

sota_methods.name: DMCHBA (Distributed Matching-by-Clone Hungarian-Based Algorithm)
sota_methods.key_idea: Implicit coordination. Agents flood their knowledge bases until they share global information. Each agent then builds a square cost matrix by cloning agents and adding pseudotasks, and solves it with the Hungarian method. Every agent computes the same conflict-free multi-task assignment without auction messages, then orders its own route locally.
sota_methods.problem: Multi-task assignment with fewer agents than tasks
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own Monte Carlo study. Also used in Lott & Honary 2026 and as a baseline in TLC-CBBA and CLAC-CBBA.
sota_methods.reported_results: Lott & Honary 2026: mean impaired MinMax 24.78 steps, second best. Lowest publication intensity, 2.08 per team step. Fastest, with ideal C_term 4.88 ms vs 1,345.6 ms for DGA. But its ideal pre-allocation median MinSum was 70.0 vs 50.0 for DGA, the worst on MinSum. UNVERIFIED (secondary summary only; full text not accessed): the original paper reportedly beats CBBA, CBHA and DRHBA on total cost and runtime over 1,000 Monte Carlo runs.
sota_methods.code_url: MATLAB File Exchange entry 181245 (listed in search results, but the page returned 404 to WebFetch, so UNVERIFIED). Reimplementations: https://github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark and https://github.com/jlott22/online-dmchba (MIT).
sota_methods.license: online-dmchba is MIT; the original is unknown
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Needs every agent to converge to the same global knowledge base (flooding), which is fragile under partitions. Poor on MinSum. It is deterministic matching followed by local ordering, not a joint route optimization.

sota_methods.name: DGA (Decentralized Genetic Algorithm)
sota_methods.key_idea: Each robot evolves a population of complete team plans (selection, crossover, mutation, repair, elitism). Robots exchange improved plans, and received plans enter the local population.
sota_methods.problem: Decentralized multi-task assignment (CV / routing)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Cao RA-L 2025; Lott & Honary 2026
sota_methods.reported_results: Lott & Honary 2026: best mean impaired MinMax at 24.49 steps, leading 18 of 24 conditions. MinSum 67.22, second. Best ideal pre-allocation medians: MinMax 21.0, MinSum 50.0. But it is the most expensive, with C_term 1.346 s and 16.25 s at 50 targets. At Bernoulli 0.5 pre-allocation only 5/100 runs were viable and 4/100 stable.
sota_methods.code_url: Reimplementation in https://github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark. Tuned with population 30 and 25 generations per update.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Heavy compute. Its reliability collapses in synchronous pre-allocation under loss. Metaheuristic, with no guarantee.

sota_methods.name: GCBBA (Global CBBA) with the Repeated Path Times utility
sota_methods.key_idea: Shows that CBBA's time-discounted-reward utility is not always DMG, and that CBBA's 50% guarantee can fail even under DMG. Proposes the Repeated Path Times utility, which is always DMG and aligned with Min-Sum and Makespan. Proposes GCBBA, which uses global consensus to restore the 50% guarantee and bounds convergence for any bundle-monotonic objective. Adds decentralized early-convergence detection.
sota_methods.problem: Multi-agent task allocation on mTSP (min-sum / makespan)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: mTSP instances in the public code; compared against CBBA and SGA (sequential greedy)
sota_methods.reported_results: Abstract: 'GCBBA significantly accelerates convergence on large-scale problems compared to the baseline CBBA.' No numbers extracted (the full PDF was not accessible) — UNVERIFIED magnitudes.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The guarantee is still only 50%. 'Global consensus' may need more communication. No evaluation under packet loss was found.

sota_methods.name: GACA (Grouping Auction-Consensus Algorithm)
sota_methods.key_idea: Keeps CBBA's two-phase auction and consensus, but bids on groups of spatially nearby tasks, formed by nearest-neighbour preprocessing. Agents can claim, partially acquire or contest groups, and consensus resolves the competing actions.
sota_methods.problem: MT-SR-IA, min-sum travel (mTSP), homogeneous agents
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own generator: 5/10/15/20 agents, 2-4 tasks per agent, 1,000 worlds per size, plus 3,280 scalability instances. Ground truth is a MILP solved with PuLP.
sota_methods.reported_results: Median percent optimality about 97% (IQR 95-99%) vs 81-84% for CBBA. Converges in the same number of iterations or fewer. All scalability cells above about 90% mean optimality.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Fully connected communication only; robustness to lossy links is untested. Only CBBA as a baseline (no PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA or GCBBA). Homogeneous agents, no time windows. Grouping ignores start positions. No code.

sota_methods.name: CC-OPI (Communication-Constrained Online PI)
sota_methods.key_idea: Event-driven online PI that interleaves negotiation with execution, so no global consensus is needed before moving. Uses cost metrics suited to dynamic topologies and a fault-tolerance layer based on version synchronization.
sota_methods.problem: UAV swarm, deadline-constrained task completion under a short communication radius (information islands)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own simulator: N in {6..16} UAVs, M = 2N or 3N tasks, 10 km field, R_c = 250 m (swept 100-800 m), 30 seeds plus 30 held-out seeds, paired bootstrap confidence intervals
sota_methods.reported_results: Task completion rate about 0.80 at R_c = 250 m. About 7 percentage points above matched online PI and CBBA, about 20 points above statically transferred baselines, and within several points of PI/CBBA under full connectivity (abstract). The per-method numbers in the HTML table extraction looked internally inconsistent — re-check them from the PDF.
sota_methods.code_url: The abstract links https://github.com/bdathe-lb/CC-OPI-Exp, which returned HTTP 404 on 2026-09-27 (not public). The related author repo https://github.com/bdathe-lb/c4-mata-sim (MIT) implements CBBA, PI and PI-Dynamic.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Ideal in-range links (packet loss only as a robustness test), synchronized clocks, no failures, dispersed initial positions. Only 6-16 UAVs. Evaluated only against PI and CBBA variants.

sota_methods.name: ED-CBBA (Event-Driven CBBA)
sota_methods.venue: arXiv 2509.06481; IEEE ICUAS 2025 (per the arXiv DOI note)
sota_methods.key_idea: Event-triggered communication for CBBA that keeps CBBA's convergence and performance bounds while sending fewer messages.
sota_methods.problem: Multi-drone surveillance and search-and-rescue under congestion
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own Monte Carlo runs
sota_methods.reported_results: Same solution quality as CBBA, with up to 52% fewer message transmissions
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Improves messages only, not solution quality. Only CBBA as a baseline.

sota_methods.name: GRAPE (anonymous hedonic game allocation)
sota_methods.key_idea: Game-theoretic coalition formation among self-interested agents with social inhibition. Converges to a Nash-stable partition in polynomial time using only local, asynchronous interactions. At least 50% suboptimality is guaranteed when social utilities are non-decreasing in coalition size.
sota_methods.problem: Large-scale swarm coalition task allocation (ST-MR-like)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own numerical experiments. Also re-implemented next to CBBA in the SPACE simulator (arXiv 2409.04230).
sota_methods.reported_results: Scalability and fast adaptation claimed (abstract). No shared-instance numbers against modern methods were found.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Guarantee holds only under specific utility monotonicity. Rarely compared head-to-head with CBBA or PI on shared instances.

sota_methods.name: Learned-bidding CBBA (Auction-Consensus with Learned Bidding Scheme)
sota_methods.venue: arXiv 2605.21932; UR 2026 (Rodriguez, Tarawneh, Koenig, Dong, Lu)
sota_methods.key_idea: Replaces CBBA's hand-crafted greedy bid with a neural bidding policy (Neural Additive Model, LSTM or Set Transformer). It is trained by RL under centralized training with decentralized execution, using MILP optima for reward shaping, and keeps CBBA's auction and consensus phases.
sota_methods.problem: Decentralized MRTA (same group and problem class as GACA)
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own instances with a MILP reference
sota_methods.reported_results: The abstract claims 'improved solution quality over classical CBBA while preserving decentralized execution'. Numbers not extracted (UNVERIFIED magnitude).
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Learned bids can break DMG, so CBBA's 50% guarantee and convergence properties are no longer guaranteed. Only CBBA as a baseline. This is the closest prior art to any 'System-1-scored CBBA' idea.

sota_methods.name: TLC-CBBA / CLAC-CBBA (clustered CBBA variants)
sota_methods.key_idea: Cluster UAVs by communication-graph centrality, then balance resources (K-medoids), then run CBBA consensus inside and between clusters. CLAC-CBBA (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838631/) adds centrality-driven adaptive clustering and load-aware self-regulation.
sota_methods.problem: Heterogeneous multi-UAV multi-task allocation at scale
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own scenarios, 12-150 UAVs
sota_methods.reported_results: TLC-CBBA: 517 vs 1,245 communication steps against Clustering-CBBA (25 tasks, 12 UAVs), score 403 vs 310 (24 UAVs, 30 tasks). CLAC-CBBA: score 425 vs 405 for TLC-CBBA (24 UAVs) and 3,207.6 vs 2,984.2 (150 UAVs), runtime 108.7 s vs 148.7 s.
sota_methods.code_url: https://github.com/ycchao0406/TLC_CBBA (TLC-CBBA); CLAC-CBBA available on request only
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: MDPI-venue papers with self-defined scores and no MILP reference. They compare only within the CBBA family plus DMCHBA.

sota_methods.name: HeteroMRTA (decentralized RL for heterogeneous coalition MRTA)
sota_methods.key_idea: An attention-based policy trained with REINFORCE and a constrained 'flashforward' mechanism. At execution each agent reactively picks its next task, so coalitions form and disband implicitly to reduce makespan.
sota_methods.problem: ST-MR heterogeneous coalition tasks (a task starts only when every required skill has arrived), makespan
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own random test sets, 50 instances each, against CTAS-D (Gurobi MILP), SAS/TACO (ant colony optimization) and a greedy heuristic
sota_methods.reported_results: SA-BT example: CTAS-D makespan 23.658 (600 s), RL(s.10) 27.193 (4.33 s), greedy 32.733. At the largest scale CTAS-D succeeds on only 4% of instances within 3,600 s, while RL succeeds on 100%. Makespan gap to the exact solution is under 23% in the worst case. More than two orders of magnitude faster.
sota_methods.code_url: https://github.com/marmotlab/HeteroMRTA (Apache-2.0); sibling https://github.com/marmotlab/DCMRTA (MIT, ICRA 2024, includes OR-Tools and CTAS-D baselines)
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Decentralized decisions still assume global state (perfect communication). No CBBA/PI baseline. Still up to 23% from MILP on small instances.

sota_methods.name: Auctions under limited communication (Otte, Kuhlman, Sofge)
sota_methods.key_idea: Analytical and experimental study of how lossy auctioneer-bidder links degrade different auction algorithms. Auctions that perform alike under perfect communication degrade differently as communication worsens.
sota_methods.problem: Auction-based MRTA under message loss
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own experiments
sota_methods.reported_results: Qualitative: the choice of auction must depend on the expected communication quality (abstract)
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Auctioneer-based rather than fully consensus-based. Pre-2021.

sota_methods.name: Distributed greedy for submodular task assignment (Qu, Brown, Li) and Distributed Hungarian (Chopra et al.)
sota_methods.key_idea: Theory-backed alternatives. A distributed version of sequential greedy for submodular utilities; the Automatica paper; the guarantee details were not extracted, so UNVERIFIED. A distributed Hungarian method (DOI 10.1109/TRO.2017.2693377) that reaches the optimal one-to-one assignment.
sota_methods.problem: Submodular multi-agent assignment; linear one-to-one assignment
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Own experiments
sota_methods.reported_results: Not extracted
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The Hungarian method is optimal only for one-to-one linear assignment, not routing. Distributed greedy inherits the approximation ratio of greedy.

benchmarks.name: CV_MRTA_Benchmark (Collaborative Visit, degraded communication; Lott & Honary 2026)
benchmarks.problem_class: Decentralized ST-SR-TA with in-schedule dependencies. Known targets, MinMax and MinSum travel. 4 robots on a 19x19 grid with 10 targets in the core; scale runs go to 34x34 and 100 targets.
benchmarks.baselines_included: CBAA, ACBBA, PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA, all under one robot shell, bus and logger
benchmarks.metrics: MinMax (S_max) and MinSum travel; publication intensity per team step; duplicate work; viability and stability of pre-allocation; full-protocol compute C_term; scale sensitivity. 25 communication conditions: ideal, Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott, Rayleigh.
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Yes, published tables. Impaired MinMax: DGA 24.49, DMCHBA 24.78, HIPC 25.12, CBAA 26.02, ACBBA 26.91, PI 29.05. Impaired MinSum: HIPC 66.95, DGA 67.22. Per-trial data (CSV.gz) are released. No formal leaderboard.
benchmarks.license: No LICENSE file (legally all rights reserved; ask the authors before redistributing a derivative)
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: Medium. The most complete public shared-instance cross-family comparison under degraded communication, with 112,500 simulations and paired statistics. But it is brand-new (arXiv, 12 Sep 2026, not peer-reviewed), from a single small lab, uses small core instances, and has no centralized or MILP reference (the authors list this as a limitation). No CBBA (only CBAA and ACBBA), and no GCBBA or GACA.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: High. Pure-Python standard-library simulator, pip install -e, smoke tests and frozen campaign plans. Easy to add a 7th allocator.

benchmarks.name: GACA MILP-referenced mTSP protocol (Rodriguez, Koenig et al. 2026)
benchmarks.problem_class: MT-SR-IA min-sum travel (mTSP), homogeneous agents, fully connected communication
benchmarks.baselines_included: CBBA and a MILP optimum (PuLP)
benchmarks.metrics: Percent of MILP optimum; iterations to converge
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Published distributions: GACA median about 97% (IQR 95-99%), CBBA 81-84% median, 5/10/15/20 agents, 1,000 worlds each
benchmarks.code_url: None released (reimplementation needed: square workspace with side U[25,55], uniform positions, 2-4 tasks per agent)
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: Medium-high for an optimality-gap claim, because a MILP reference is what reviewers accept. Weakened by the missing code and the single baseline.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Medium. Generator and MILP are easy to rebuild. Use Gurobi or HiGHS with time limits for 20 agents and 80 tasks.

benchmarks.name: GCBBA mTSP testbed (ECAI 2025)
benchmarks.problem_class: mTSP min-sum / makespan allocation
benchmarks.baselines_included: CBBA, GCBBA, SGA (centralized sequential greedy)
benchmarks.metrics: Objective value and convergence iterations/time
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Paper at https://ebooks.iospress.nl/doi/10.3233/FAIA251222. Qualitative claim: significantly faster convergence than CBBA. Numbers not extracted.
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: Medium (peer-reviewed at ECAI, and it is the strongest theory-grounded CBBA variant)
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: High. Python with numpy and networkx.

benchmarks.name: Cao et al. RA-L 2025 non-ideal-communication CV comparison
benchmarks.problem_class: Multi-UAV collaborative visit, pre-allocation and dynamic allocation, with packet loss, bit errors and delay, in synchronous and asynchronous modes
benchmarks.baselines_included: CBAA, CBBA, HIPC, PI, DHBA, DGA
benchmarks.metrics: MinMax path quality, reliability (conflicts), payload-aware communication overhead, runtime. 100 Monte Carlo runs per case at two scales.
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Published (IEEE abstract): CBBA is best in pre-allocation on reliability, overhead and efficiency, and best on optimality in dynamic allocation. DHBA is more reliable with lower overhead in harsh communication. Bit errors cause conflicting allocations.
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: High as a peer-reviewed comparison. Low as a reusable benchmark without code.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Low-medium (the protocol must be reimplemented from the paper)

benchmarks.name: Nayak et al. RA-L 2020 imperfect-communication comparison
benchmarks.problem_class: Decentralized task allocation under Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott and Rayleigh fading communication
benchmarks.baselines_included: CBAA, ACBBA, DHBA, HIPC, PI
benchmarks.metrics: Maximum-agent travel and maximum-agent message count, 50 random instances per condition
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Published. Main finding (as summarized in Lott 2026): the best route allocator and the best communication allocator differ.
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: High as the canonical comparison under degraded communication, but dated
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Low (no code found)

benchmarks.name: HeteroMRTA / DCMRTA test sets (heterogeneous coalition MRTA with MILP baseline)
benchmarks.problem_class: ST-MR heterogeneous coalition tasks, makespan
benchmarks.baselines_included: CTAS-D (Gurobi MILP), SAS, TACO (ACO), greedy, RL; DCMRTA adds OR-Tools
benchmarks.metrics: Success rate, makespan, average waiting time, computation time, ability redundancy
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Published tables in RA-L 2025 (e.g., SA-BT: CTAS-D 23.658, RL(s.10) 27.193, greedy 32.733)
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: High in the learned-MRTA community (RA-L and ICRA, public code, MILP baseline). No communication degradation and no CBBA-family baselines.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Medium. The test-set generator and baselines ship with the code; CTAS-D needs Gurobi.

benchmarks.name: League of Robot Runners 2024 Benchmark Archive (lifelong task scheduling plus MAPF)
benchmarks.problem_class: Centralized lifelong multi-robot task scheduling and path planning (errands), 100-10,000 agents, warehouse, sortation, city and game maps
benchmarks.baselines_included: Best-known solutions from 50 teams (1,513 submissions in 2024/25), with linked implementations in the Code-Archive
benchmarks.metrics: Total tasks finished within a simulation time and a per-step compute limit
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Yes. Best-known solution table, e.g., MR24-WAREHOUSE 154,834 tasks with 10,000 agents; MR24-RANDOM-01 696 tasks with 100 agents.
benchmarks.license: Start-Kit MIT; the Benchmark-Archive has no license file
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: Very high as a benchmark (Amazon-sponsored, public best-known solutions). But it is centralized, so a decentralized allocator would claim 'near best-known with bounded communication', not SOTA.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Medium-low (C++ start kit; path planning dominates the results)

benchmarks.name: Classical OR instance libraries: Solomon VRPTW and Chao Team Orienteering (TOP/TOPTW)
benchmarks.problem_class: Centralized vehicle routing with time windows and team orienteering (a reward-collecting analogue of CBBA's time-discounted scoring)
benchmarks.baselines_included: Best-known solutions from decades of OR literature. TOP and OPTW instance sets are also at https://www.mech.kuleuven.be/en/cib/op
benchmarks.metrics: Distance, vehicles, collected score
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Yes (best-known solution tables)
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: High for an optimality-gap claim. No decentralized CBBA/PI paper reporting on these instances turned up in this sweep, so it is an unused but credible yardstick.
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: High (plain-text instances)

open_gaps: No accepted decentralized-MRTA leaderboard exists. Only three cross-family comparisons use shared instances (Nayak RA-L 2020, Cao RA-L 2025, Lott & Honary arXiv 2026), and they rank methods differently. Only Lott's code and data are public, and that repo has no license.

No paper reports optimality gaps against a MILP or best-known reference under degraded communication. GACA has a MILP reference but full connectivity only. Lott has degraded communication but lists 'centralized references' as future work. The optimality-vs-link-quality curve is unmeasured.

No allocator leads both objectives. Under impaired communication, DGA and DMCHBA lead MinMax while HIPC and DGA lead MinSum. DMCHBA is the most frugal (2.08 publications per step, 4.88 ms) but worst on ideal MinSum (70.0 vs 50.0 for DGA). DGA is best on quality but costs 1.35-16 s and its synchronous pre-allocation collapses under loss (5/100 viable at p=0.5).

CBBA's theoretical footing is weaker than usually cited. Kha et al. (ECAI 2025) show the standard time-discounted score is not always DMG and the 50% guarantee can fail. Learned bidding (Rodriguez et al. 2026) drops the guarantee entirely.
The gap to MILP is real and measurable only for CBBA: median 81-84% of optimum on min-sum mTSP (GACA 2026). No published MILP gap was found for PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA or GRAPE on shared instances.

Most 2024-2026 variants (ED-CBBA, TLC-CBBA, CLAC-CBBA, GACA, CC-OPI, learned-bid CBBA) compare only against CBBA or PI and their own ablations. Most release no code: GACA none, CC-OPI a 404 link, CLAC-CBBA on request. Claims cannot be checked against each other.

Learned decentralized allocators (HeteroMRTA RA-L 2025, DAN DARS 2022, MAGNNET IV 2025) assume perfect communication or global state at execution. They never benchmark against the CBBA/PI family, and they remain 7-23% from exact solvers on small instances.
Synchronous pre-allocation reliability under loss is a separate failure mode from route quality. Under loss, ACBBA, PI and DGA lose viability; HIPC and DMCHBA do not. Most papers report only quality.

Bundle or planning depth is tuned for ideal networks. Lott & Honary (arXiv 2609.06273) show the MinSum-optimal bundle length moves from B=12 to B=2 at 25% loss, with 7-14% penalties when ideal-network settings are kept. No allocator adapts depth online to link quality.

Heterogeneous, tightly coupled coalition tasks (ST-MR) under degraded communication are unaddressed. CBGA (Hunt et al., Cognitive Computation 2014, DOI 10.1007/s12559-014-9265-0) and GRAPE predate modern loss models, and HeteroMRTA ignores communication.

sota_opportunities.idea: Loss-adaptive hybrid allocator: HIPC-style implicit team prediction plus DMCHBA-style clone-Hungarian seeding plus a cheap decentralized local-search repair (PI-style removal and insertion with the 2023 deadlock guard), with planning depth B adapted online to the measured packet-delivery ratio. Aim: be the first method to Pareto-dominate on both MinMax and MinSum across the 24 impaired conditions at DMCHBA-like message cost.
sota_opportunities.target_benchmark: CV_MRTA_Benchmark (Lott & Honary 2026), all 25 conditions plus its scale campaign, reusing its paired instances, statistics pipeline and six frozen baselines
sota_opportunities.why_gap_exists: Each existing method sits in a different operating region: DGA/DMCHBA on MinMax, HIPC/DGA on MinSum, DMCHBA on communication and compute, HIPC/DMCHBA on reliability. The same authors show the best B depends on loss, but no allocator adapts it.
sota_opportunities.baselines_to_beat: Impaired MinMax: DGA 24.49, DMCHBA 24.78. Impaired MinSum: HIPC 66.95, DGA 67.22. Publications: DMCHBA 2.08 per team step. Reliability at Bernoulli p=0.5: HIPC and DMCHBA 100/100 viable and stable. Compute: DMCHBA 4.88 ms.
sota_opportunities.risk: High statistical risk. Core instances are tiny (4 robots, 10 targets), and the leaders are separated by about 0.3 steps with many non-significant pairwise tests. A new method may tie, which is the same failure mode as CBJA's VOC-vs-deadline-rule equivalence. Pre-register non-inferiority margins, and emphasize the larger-scale campaign (up to 100 targets) where the spread is bigger. The repo has no license, so get the authors' permission or reimplement.

sota_opportunities.idea: Guarantee-preserving learned bidding. A neural (or System-1) scorer constrained to be monotone and DMG by construction, for example a submodular-structured or deep-set concave-of-modular marginal-gain head, plugged into GCBBA's global-consensus loop. Add grouped bids (GACA-style) and a post-consensus decentralized 2-opt/swap phase. This keeps the 50% certificate while closing the MILP gap.
sota_opportunities.target_benchmark: GACA's MILP-referenced mTSP protocol (reimplemented: 5-20 agents, 1,000 worlds per size, exact MILP via Gurobi/HiGHS) and the GCBBA public mTSP code. Extension: time-window variants with Solomon/TOPTW-derived instances and best-known references.
sota_opportunities.why_gap_exists: CBBA reaches 81-84% of optimum. GACA reaches about 97% but without code, and with full connectivity, homogeneous agents and no guarantee. Learned-bid CBBA (2026) gains quality but gives up DMG and convergence guarantees. GCBBA restores the guarantee but was not shown to improve quality.
sota_opportunities.baselines_to_beat: GACA median about 97% of MILP (IQR 95-99%). CBBA 81-84%. GCBBA and SGA from the public repo. Learned-bid CBBA (reimplement; no numbers extracted).
sota_opportunities.risk: There is only about 3 points of headroom on GACA's own instances, so the claim has to move to harder regimes (time windows, heterogeneity, 20+ agents with 80+ tasks, lossy links) where headroom exists. The Koenig/Rodriguez group is actively publishing in exactly this direction (GACA, learned bidding, MRS 2025 loss mechanism), so the risk of being scooped is high. A GACA reimplementation may be challenged as unfaithful.

sota_opportunities.idea: First optimality-gap-vs-link-quality study with a new allocator. Attach a MILP/best-known reference (Gurobi or LKH-3) to every degraded-communication condition and report percent-of-optimal curves for CBBA, GCBBA, GACA, PI, HIPC, DMCHBA, DGA, CC-OPI-style online PI and the proposed method. The new method's pitch is 'closest to optimal at every loss level'.
sota_opportunities.target_benchmark: CV_MRTA_Benchmark instances plus the GACA generator, run under Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott and Rayleigh loss (Lott's channel models)
sota_opportunities.why_gap_exists: Lott explicitly omits centralized references. GACA and Cao never cross MILP gaps with loss models. Reviewers accept percent-of-optimal numbers more readily than raw step counts on a self-built simulator, which was the main weakness of the CBJA paper.
sota_opportunities.baselines_to_beat: The same numbers as the two opportunities above, now expressed as a percent-of-optimal curve
sota_opportunities.risk: On its own this is benchmark or analysis work, which repeats the AAMAS-2027 outcome. It becomes a SOTA paper only if bundled with a method that wins the curve. MILP is tractable only at small scale; use Gurobi time limits and report best bound plus gap.

sota_opportunities.idea: Consensus-based coalition allocator for heterogeneous ST-MR tasks under lossy communication (CBGA or GRAPE successor), compared directly against decentralized RL and MILP on public test sets
sota_opportunities.target_benchmark: HeteroMRTA and DCMRTA test sets (marmotlab, Apache-2.0/MIT) with CTAS-D (Gurobi) and OR-Tools baselines, plus a lossy-communication variant
sota_opportunities.why_gap_exists: HeteroMRTA is the strongest public learned allocator but assumes perfect information at execution and is still up to 23% from MILP. The CBBA-family coalition methods (CBGA 2014, GRAPE 2018) were never evaluated on these sets or under modern loss models.
sota_opportunities.baselines_to_beat: SA-BT (kn=9 example): CTAS-D makespan 23.658 (600 s), RL(s.10) 27.193 (4.33 s), greedy 32.733. At large scale CTAS-D succeeds on only 4% within 1 h, while RL succeeds on 100%.
sota_opportunities.risk: Coalition synchronization (wait-for-all-skills) is hard for consensus methods, and deadlocks are common. Beating RL(s.10) makespan while respecting communication limits may need a GPU-trained component; the 4x H100 budget is sufficient for that.

sota_opportunities.idea: Online, partition-tolerant PI/CBBA hybrid for deadline tasks in the CC-OPI setting (short radius, information islands). Combine version-vector state sync with HIPC prediction and loss-adaptive depth.
sota_opportunities.target_benchmark: CC-OPI protocol (6-16 UAVs, M = 2N/3N, R_c 100-800 m, 30 plus 30 seeds), reimplemented, with the MIT c4-mata-sim (CBBA, PI, PI-Dynamic built in) as a harness
sota_opportunities.why_gap_exists: CC-OPI is only 10 days old, has no public code (404), assumes ideal in-range links and synchronized clocks, and compares only against PI and CBBA variants.
sota_opportunities.baselines_to_beat: CC-OPI task completion rate about 0.80 at R_c = 250 m. Matched online PI and CBBA are about 7 points lower, and static transfer about 20 points lower (abstract numbers).
sota_opportunities.risk: The baseline can't be reproduced without the authors' code. Small scale. A reviewer may see it as incremental over PI. c4-mata-sim is a student contest project with low credibility on its own.

sweeps.area: Learning-based multi-robot / multi-agent task allocation and routing, 2021-2026: GNN, attention and transformer policies, multi-agent neural combinatorial optimization, MARL, imitation of optimal solvers, learned bidding inside CBBA, and LLM-evolved heuristics. The review focuses on decentralized, communication-limited, online settings. Bottom line: no learned method is verified SOTA on an established public multi-robot allocation benchmark under degraded communication. Learned solvers lead mainly on synthetic, centralized, uniform-distribution instances with speed-quality trade-offs. Classical OR (LKH3, HGA, HGS, AILS-II) still holds the public instance libraries (mTSPLib, CVRPLIB X/XL). Where MILP can be solved, it beats learned MRTA policies, and at larger team sizes a plain greedy rule does too.

sota_methods.name: PARCO (Parallel AutoRegressive Combinatorial Optimization)
sota_methods.venue: NeurIPS 2025 (as stated on the arXiv abstract page)
sota_methods.problem: Multi-agent combinatorial optimization: min-max heterogeneous CVRP (HCVRP), open multi-depot capacitated pickup-and-delivery (OMDCPDP), and flexible flow shop (FFSP)
sota_methods.key_idea: All M agents choose actions at the same time at each construction step, using transformer communication layers between agents, multiple pointers, and a learned-priority conflict handler. Construction steps drop from the sum of per-agent steps to the maximum.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Synthetic uniform instances only, no CVRPLIB. HCVRP N in {60,100}, M in {3,5,7}; OMDCPDP N in {50,100}, M up to 20; FFSP N up to 100. Zero-shot tests reach N=1000, M=200.
sota_methods.reported_results: HCVRP N=100, M=5: SISR 6.17 (reference, 623 s); 2D-Ptr greedy 6.75 (+9.4%); Equity-Transformer greedy 7.25 (+17.5%); DPN greedy 6.94 (+12.48%); PARCO greedy 6.61 (+7.13%, 0.05 s); PARCO sampling 6.36 (+3.08%). OMDCPDP N=100, M=15: OR-Tools (60 s) 51.49; PARCO greedy 51.45; PARCO sampling 49.69, which is the reference. The paper reports 3.3x to 24.7x speedups over sequential autoregressive baselines.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Construction is centralized. The communication layers assume perfect, instant all-to-all information, and there is no message loss, delay or partial observability. It still trails the classical SISR heuristic on HCVRP (+3.08% at best). There are no public-library instances. The GeoPAR follow-up (arXiv 2609.00577, Sep 2026, no code found) says parallel AR solvers generalize poorly at large scale.

sota_methods.name: Equity-Transformer (ET)
sota_methods.license: not checked (verified: repo exists and is linked as the reproducible code)
sota_methods.problem: Min-max mTSP and min-max multi-agent pickup-and-delivery (mPDP)
sota_methods.key_idea: Recasts min-max multi-agent routing as sequential generation by one transformer, with inductive biases (equity context) that spread workload evenly across agents.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Synthetic uniform instances up to 1000 cities and 100 vehicles
sota_methods.reported_results: Abstract, verbatim: 'significant reductions of runtime, approximately 335 times, and cost values of about 53% compared to a competitive heuristic (LKH3) in the case of 100 vehicles with 1,000 cities of mTSP'.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The headline win is against LKH3, a general-purpose heuristic, at large m. The dedicated min-max mTSP hybrid genetic algorithm (HGA; Mahmoudinazlou & Kwon, C&OR 2024, arXiv 2307.07120) appeared after ET's arXiv v1, and I did not verify whether ET was ever compared against it. Later work (GaS, 2508.17087) shows ET behind LKH3 at small m: n=50, m=2 gives ET x128 3.2079 vs LKH3 (600 s) 3.1517. Decoding is centralized.

sota_methods.name: DPN (Decoupling Partition and Navigation)
sota_methods.problem: Min-max VRP with single and multiple depots (min-max mTSP and variants)
sota_methods.key_idea: A Partition-and-Navigation encoder learns separate embeddings for splitting customers among routes and for ordering each route. Adds an agent-permutation-symmetric (APS) loss and rotation-based positional encoding.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Synthetic uniform instances. I could not verify whether public libraries were tested.
sota_methods.reported_results: Claims to significantly beat earlier learning-based min-max solvers. Third-party numbers from GaS (arXiv 2508.17087): n=50, m=2 DPN x128 3.1949 vs LKH3 (600 s) 3.1517; n=100, m=2 DPN x128 4.1774 vs LKH3 4.0694.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Still loses to LKH3 when m is small. It is centralized and assumes a static, fully observed instance.

sota_methods.name: GaS (Generate-and-Split: learning-based path generation plus optimal splitting for min-max mTSP)
sota_methods.license: no LICENSE file found at repo root
sota_methods.venue: arXiv 2508.17087. ECAI 2025 is inferred from the repo name only (unverified).
sota_methods.problem: Min-max mTSP
sota_methods.key_idea: RL generates one giant tour. An exact or learned splitting step then divides it into m tours minimizing the longest tour, so the network never has to reason about agents directly.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Uniform random n=50 to 500, m=2 to 50, plus out-of-distribution rotation, Gaussian and explosion distributions
sota_methods.reported_results: Better than the best learning-based method (ET or DPN) in 13 of 18 configurations (p<0.05), and better on 90.7% of out-of-distribution cases. n=50, m=2: GaS 3.1918, DPN 3.1949, ET 3.2079, LKH3 (600 s) 3.1517.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The authors state LKH3 stays better, especially at small m. Centralized, static.

sota_methods.name: ScheduleNet (min-max mTSP with RL; also arXiv 2106.03051)
sota_methods.problem: Min-max mTSP, including limited-observation and online variants
sota_methods.key_idea: Agent-task graph with type-aware graph attention and a decentralized semi-MDP policy trained with an episodic makespan reward
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Random instances plus mTSPLib (Necula et al.: eil51, berlin52, eil76, rat99 with m=2,3,5,7)
sota_methods.reported_results: mTSPLib average makespan relative to CPLEX (Table 3): LKH3 1.00; OR-Tools 1.03; ScheduleNet greedy 1.13, sampling-64 1.05; DAN greedy 1.18, sampling-64 1.11.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Learned policies are 5-18% worse than LKH3 on the only standard public mTSP set, and DAN drops sharply on non-uniform instances (berlin52). This is direct evidence that learned min-max solvers are not SOTA on public instances.

sota_methods.name: HeteroMRTA (Heterogeneous Multi-robot Task Allocation and Scheduling via RL)
sota_methods.venue: IEEE RA-L vol. 10, no. 3, pp. 2654-2661, 2025 (Dai, Rai, Chiun, Cao, Sartoretti)
sota_methods.problem: Heterogeneous single-task-robot / multi-robot-task (ST-MR) allocation. Coalitions must gather before a task starts; the objective is makespan.
sota_methods.key_idea: Attention-based policy trained with REINFORCE and a POMO-style baseline. Each agent picks its next task sequentially and independently, conditioned on earlier agents' choices.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Self-generated test set, shipped as RALTestSet in the repo
sota_methods.reported_results: Small SA-BT case (Table I): CTAS-D (Gurobi MILP, 600 s) makespan 23.66; RL sampling-10 27.19; RL greedy 29.00; Greedy 32.73; SAS 27.41; TACO 35.07. Larger case: CTAS-D solves only 4% of instances within 3600 s, RL sampling-10 35.48 vs Greedy 43.96.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The paper states the formulation is 'decentralized sequential decision-making problem with global communication', i.e., perfect broadcast is assumed. About 15-23% worse than MILP wherever MILP finishes. Tested by Sadcher (below): it loses to greedy on large teams.

sota_methods.name: SADCHER (Scheduling using Attention-based Dynamic Coalitions of Heterogeneous Robots)
sota_methods.license: code: no LICENSE file found; dataset licence not verified
sota_methods.problem: Real-time heterogeneous MRTA with dynamic coalitions and precedence constraints (makespan)
sota_methods.key_idea: Imitation learning from 250,000 optimal MILP schedules. Graph attention plus a transformer predict robot-task rewards, and relaxed bipartite matching turns them into feasible assignments.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Its own 250K optimal-schedule dataset and 500 unseen instances (8 tasks, 3 robots, 3 precedences). Scaling tests at N=3/5/20 robots and M=6-250 tasks.
sota_methods.reported_results: Mean gap to MILP optimum: S-Sadcher 3.8%, Sadcher 6.8%, S-HeteroMRTA 10.8%, Greedy 20.4%, HeteroMRTA 21.5%. Sadcher beats HeteroMRTA on 80.6% of instances. At N=20 robots, Greedy beats S-Sadcher once M>70. Per-decision time is at most 80 ms for Sadcher and at most 3 ms for Greedy.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Centralized and fully observed. It needs expensive optimal demonstrations, so large teams are out of distribution, and the authors say the advantage is lost for bigger teams. The '250K' set is one lab's released dataset, not a community benchmark with a leaderboard.

sota_methods.name: NDS (Neural Deconstruction Search)
sota_methods.problem: CVRP, VRPTW and prize-collecting VRP (single fleet; not multi-robot allocation)
sota_methods.key_idea: A neural policy picks which customers to remove from the current solution, and a simple greedy insertion rebuilds it, inside an iterative search. A learned destroy operator plus a classical repair operator.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Synthetic uniform instances N=100/500/1000/2000. No CVRPLIB X results.
sota_methods.reported_results: Same time budget as the classical baseline: CVRP500 -0.20% vs HGS (60 s); CVRP1000 -0.90% (120 s); CVRP2000 -2.34% (240 s); CVRP100 +0.04%. VRPTW1000 -3.14% vs PyVRP; PCVRP1000 -4.71% vs PyVRP.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The strongest verified 'learned beats HGS' claim, but only on uniform synthetic instances with short time budgets and a GPU. It is untested on CVRPLIB X/XL, where the 2026 survey (arXiv 2602.21761) finds neural solvers generally worse than SOTA heuristics. Single-fleet, centralized. No min-max or multi-robot communication version exists, which is an opportunity.

sota_methods.name: Learned-bidding CBBA (Auction-Consensus Algorithm with Learned Bidding Scheme)
sota_methods.venue: arXiv preprint, May 2026 (Rodriguez, Tarawneh, Koenig, Dong, Lu)
sota_methods.problem: Decentralized single-task-robot / single-robot-task (ST-SR) MRTA with time-extended assignment and min-sum travel
sota_methods.key_idea: Replaces CBBA's hand-written greedy bid with a neural bid (NAM, LSTM or Set Transformer) trained by PPO. The reward mixes team distance, coverage and agreement with MILP-optimal solutions, and CBBA's consensus phase is kept.
sota_methods.benchmark_used: 1000 random 2D worlds (5 agents, 10-20 tasks), then larger teams
sota_methods.reported_results: NAM reaches about 90% optimality at 5 agents and about 87% at 20 agents but hits convergence timeouts. LSTM is about 5% better than CBBA at small scale and degrades with more agents. LSTM needs 11-13 consensus iterations vs 6-9 for CBBA. Transformer variants failed to learn.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The closest prior work to CBJA's lineage. Gains are small, do not hold at scale, and slow consensus, which hurts under lossy links. No packet-loss experiments. A sibling paper, GACA (arXiv 2608.15884), gets about 97% median optimality vs 81-84% for CBBA with no learning at all, just spatial task grouping. That is a warning that a simple structural fix can beat learned bids.

sota_methods.name: MDGAM + GRMAPG (communication-constrained cooperative task scheduling)
sota_methods.problem: Distributed heterogeneous task scheduling with time windows and range-limited communication
sota_methods.key_idea: A multi-decoder graph attention model that updates node and edge features, trained without a critic using group-relative advantages computed over equivalent task-planning instances
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Self-generated: 50 tasks/4 agents, 100/7, 150/10. Communication radius r in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6}.
sota_methods.reported_results: Medium scale, r=0.4: 82.90 tasks completed vs 79.61 for PI-maxAss (+4.13%), and +3.74% vs CAM. Large scale: +5.94% and +5.06%. Baselines were CBBA, PI-maxAss, EEPI, DL-DRL and CAM.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: The paper states that 'bandwidth, delay, and packet loss are not explicitly modeled' (range only). Gains over the best classical method are small (4-6%), and it uses a self-made testbed.

sota_methods.name: MAPF-GPT (and the MAPF-GPT-DDG fine-tune)
sota_methods.problem: Decentralized, communication-free multi-agent pathfinding (coordination layer, not allocation)
sota_methods.key_idea: Transformer imitation learning on about 1B observation-action pairs from LaCAM expert solutions over 3.75M POGEMA instances
sota_methods.benchmark_used: POGEMA benchmark maps
sota_methods.reported_results: Claims to beat the best learnable MAPF solvers (SCRIMP, DCC, Follower). I did not extract exact numbers.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Veerapaneni et al. (arXiv 2409.14491) show that simple imitation learning plus a CS-PIBT collision shield, trained in minutes, 'dramatically outperforms existing ML MAPF policies' and that large-scale imitation learning alone 'does not produce impressive results'. Lesson: learned policy plus a cheap classical safety or repair layer beats scale.

sota_methods.name: SILLM (Scalable Imitation Learning for Lifelong MAPF)
sota_methods.problem: Lifelong MAPF at warehouse scale (up to 10,000 agents)
sota_methods.key_idea: GPU-accelerated imitation-learning policy with a communication module, collision resolution and global guidance
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Six large maps including League of Robot Runners (LoRR) settings
sota_methods.reported_results: +137.7% average throughput vs learning-based methods, +16.0% vs search-based methods, and better than the 2023 LoRR winner (as reported in the abstract)
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Covers path planning only; task assignment is given. Centralized GPU inference. I found no verified entry of it in the LoRR scheduler track.

sota_methods.name: LLM-evolved heuristics: ReEvo (NeurIPS 2024), MCTS-AHD (ICML 2025), EoH (ICML 2024), FunSearch
sota_methods.problem: Automatic heuristic design for TSP, CVRP (ACO, GLS, POMO/LEHD plug-ins), bin packing, knapsack, orienteering, and similar problems
sota_methods.key_idea: An LLM acts as the mutation and crossover operator over executable heuristic code, adding reflection (ReEvo), natural-language 'thoughts' (EoH) or tree search over programs (MCTS-AHD).
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Synthetic TSP/CVRP/BPP/KP instances
sota_methods.reported_results: MCTS-AHD, stepwise-constructive TSP with GPT-4o-mini: gap 9.69% / 11.79% / 13.71% at N=50/100/200, vs EoH 12.67% / 14.49% / 16.68%.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: None of these covers multi-agent, min-max, decentralized or communication-limited allocation (ReEvo's README lists no mTSP). Evolved constructive heuristics remain about 10-14% from optimal on TSP. I found no verified work that LLM-evolves CBBA or PI bid/consensus rules under lossy communication.

sota_methods.name: Baty et al. ML-plus-combinatorial-optimization pipeline (EURO Meets NeurIPS 2022 dynamic VRPTW winner)
sota_methods.venue: arXiv 2304.00789; ranked first in the EURO Meets NeurIPS 2022 Vehicle Routing Competition, per its abstract
sota_methods.problem: Online / dynamic VRPTW with dispatching waves
sota_methods.key_idea: Structured learning: a statistical model parameterizes a combinatorial-optimization layer (a prize-collecting VRP solved by an HGS-type solver) instead of an end-to-end deep RL policy
sota_methods.benchmark_used: EURO Meets NeurIPS 2022 dynamic track, real ORTEC data
sota_methods.reported_results: First place in the competition (abstract). I did not extract per-instance numbers.
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Single-depot fleet dispatch, centralized. It is still the strongest public evidence that in dynamic settings ML wins as a guide for an optimization layer, not as an end-to-end policy. The organizers wrote beforehand that the ML community 'generally uses deep learning, but fails to outperform OR baselines'.

sota_methods.name: CapAM (Capsule Attention for MRTA)
sota_methods.problem: MRTA with task deadlines and workloads and robot capacity limits (online)
sota_methods.key_idea: Capsule-network node encoder plus attention decoder plus a context module, trained with REINFORCE
sota_methods.benchmark_used: Self-generated scenarios
sota_methods.reported_results: Abstract: better task completion and more than 10x faster decisions than non-learning online MRTA methods. Exact numbers and baseline names not extracted (unverified).
sota_methods.weaknesses_or_gaps: Older (pre-2023), self-made testbed, centralized decoding, no communication model

benchmarks.name: mTSPLib (Necula et al., min-max mTSP)
benchmarks.url: http://profs.info.uaic.ro/~mtsplib/MinMaxMTSP/ (URL from search results; page not fetched directly)
benchmarks.problem_class: Static min-max mTSP: eil51, berlin52, eil76, rat99 with m=2,3,5,7 (16 instances)
benchmarks.metrics: Longest-tour length; gap to CPLEX optimum or bound
benchmarks.baselines_included: CPLEX, LKH3, OR-Tools, DAN, ScheduleNet. HGA (github.com/Sasanm88/m-TSP) and RL-CMSA (arXiv 2602.23579) also use TSPLIB-derived sets.
benchmarks.has_leaderboard_or_published_numbers: Yes, published numbers (ScheduleNet AAMAS 2023 Table 3), but no live leaderboard
benchmarks.ease_of_adoption: Very easy (16 small instances), but tiny, and LKH3 already reaches the CPLEX values, so there is little room to show SOTA.
benchmarks.credibility_for_sota_claim: Medium for min-max mTSP. Irrelevant to decentralized or communication-limited claims.

benchmarks.name: CVRPLIB (X, XL, Golden, Solomon VRPTW, etc.) plus the 2026 XL BKS Challenge
benchmarks.problem_class: Static CVRP and VRPTW (single fleet, centralized)
benchmarks.metrics: Distance; gap to best-known solution (BKS), proven-optimal flags
